entry.title: HARICOT: De Novo Assembly of Raw Nanopore Signals using Fuzzy de Bruijn Graphs
entry.summary:
Nanopore sequencing enables reading long nucleotide sequences by measuring characteristic changes in ionic current as molecules pass through a nanopore. These current measurements, known as raw signals, can be analyzed without translating them into bases (i.e., without basecalling), which provides fast and resource-efficient genome analysis. Prior work, Rawsamble, enables finding overlaps between raw nanopore signals, without basecalling them, and generating assemblies from these overlaps with off-the-shelf assemblers such as miniasm.

Source: bioRxiv Bioinformatics Preprints · Tags: #bioinformatics #genomics-proteins #combinatorics

entry.title: CATEomics: model selection and ensembling for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation from high-dimensional omics data
entry.summary:
CATEomics addresses the lack of a standardized and reproducible process for choosing among conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimators in high-dimensional omics studies, where their estimation errors cannot be evaluated directly from observed outcomes. The R package accepts a SummarizedExperiment, applies common preprocessing and data partitions across R and Python estimators, compares their out-of-fold estimates using proxy losses, supports model selection and ensembling, and returns the resulting CATE estimates to the original object for downstream omics analysis. Availability and implementation: CATEomics is implemented in R and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/matsui-lab/CATEomics.

Source: bioRxiv Bioinformatics Preprints · Tags: #bioinformatics #genomics-proteins

entry.title: Minimizing data requirements for chemical and material property prediction via cluster-based training set selection
entry.summary:
Nature Computational Science, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s43588-026-01076-9 A survey of 100 algorithms across 60 chemical and materials property prediction tasks finds that cluster-based selection of training data outperforms active learning, and a theoretical framework establishes why this occurs in the low-data limit.
